details:
**"Harlem" ("What happens to a dream deferred?")**
Hughes's short 1951 poem, also called "Dream Deferred," from the collection Montage of a Dream Deferred. It asks whether a deferred dream will "dry up / like a raisin in the sun," "fester like a sore," "stink like rotten meat," or "crust and sugar over— / like a syrupy sweet," suggests "maybe it just sags / like a heavy load," and ends with the italicized question "Or does it explode?"

**A Raisin in the Sun**
Lorraine Hansberry's 1959 play takes its title from the line "like a raisin in the sun" in "Harlem," and the poem serves as its epigraph. It is a common way to link Hughes to other authors.

**"The Weary Blues"**
The title poem of Hughes's first collection (1926). The speaker hears a Black musician playing a "drowsy syncopated tune" "down on Lenox Avenue the other night" "by the pale dull pallor of an old gas light," swaying "on his rickety stool" with "ebony hands on each ivory key," his foot going "thump, thump, thump." The poem ends as "the stars went out and so did the moon" and the singer "slept like a rock or a man that's dead."

**"The Negro Speaks of Rivers"**
Hughes's early poem, written as a teenager, in which the speaker says, "I've known rivers ancient as the world and older than the flow of human blood in human veins." He "bathed in the Euphrates when dawns were young," built his hut near the Congo, which "lulled me to sleep," raised the pyramids above the Nile, and heard the singing of the Mississippi, seeing "its muddy bosom turn all golden in the sunset." Its refrain is "My soul has grown deep like the rivers."

**"I, Too"**
A poem in which the speaker declares, "I, too, sing America. / I am the darker brother. / They send me to eat in the kitchen / When company comes." He predicts that "tomorrow, / I'll be at the table," and that "they'll see how beautiful I am / And be ashamed," ending, "I, too, am America." It responds to Walt Whitman's "I Hear America Singing."

**"Theme for English B"**
A poem framed as an assignment from a college instructor who tells the class, "Go home and write a page tonight. / And let that page come out of you." The speaker, the only Black student in his class, writes that he likes "to eat, sleep, drink, and be in love," "to work, read, learn, and understand life," and wants "a pipe for a Christmas present, / or records—Bessie, bop, or Bach." He tells the white instructor, "As I learn from you, / I guess you learn from me."

**"Mother to Son"**
A dramatic monologue in which a mother tells her son, "Life for me ain't been no crystal stair." Her staircase has had "tacks in it, / And splinters, / And boards torn up, / And places with no carpet on the floor," but she has kept "climbin' on," and she urges him not to turn back.

**Montage of a Dream Deferred and "Dream Boogie"**
Hughes's 1951 book-length poem sequence about Harlem, structured like bebop jazz, which contains "Harlem." It opens with "Dream Boogie," which begins "Good morning, daddy! / Ain't you heard / The boogie-woogie rumble / Of a dream deferred?" and is interrupted by an italic voice asking, "You think / It's a happy beat?"

**"Let America Be America Again"**
A 1935 poem in which the speaker longs for America to "be the dream it used to be," while a parenthetical voice interjects, "America never was America to me." The speaker identifies himself as the poor white, the Negro, the Native American, and the immigrant, saying "I am the man who sailed those early seas," and answers the question of who he is with phrases like "the worker sold to the machine." It ends with the call to "make America again!"

**"Dreams" ("Hold fast to dreams")**
A short poem urging the reader to "hold fast to dreams," for "if dreams die / Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly," and "when dreams go / Life is a barren field / Frozen with snow." Dreams are one of Hughes's central themes, also appearing in "As I Grew Older," which begins "It was a long time ago. / I have almost forgotten my dream" and describes a wall rising "between me and my dream."

**"Ballad of the Landlord"**
A poem in which a tenant complains to his landlord about a leaking roof and broken steps and refuses to pay rent. When he threatens the landlord, the landlord shouts "Police! Police! / Come and get this man! / He's trying to ruin the government / And overturn the land!" and the tenant is jailed, ending in newspaper-style headlines.

**Lenox Avenue and the Harlem Renaissance**
Hughes was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance, the 1920s flowering of African American art centered in Harlem, New York. His poetry draws on blues and jazz rhythms and is often set on Harlem's Lenox Avenue.

**The Big Sea ("Beyond Sandy Hook")**
Hughes's 1940 autobiography. Its opening chapter, "Beyond Sandy Hook," describes him throwing his books into the sea as he sailed to Africa as a ship's crewman. He also recounts being "discovered" by the poet Vachel Lindsay after leaving poems by Lindsay's plate while working as a busboy at a Washington, D.C., hotel.

**Fine Clothes to the Jew and other poems ("Life Is Fine," "Tired," "Note on Commercial Theatre")**
Fine Clothes to the Jew (1927) is Hughes's second poetry collection, which draws on the blues. In "Life Is Fine," a man fails to drown himself and later "took the elevator / Sixteen floors above the ground" but doesn't jump, concluding "Life is fine! / Fine as wine!" "Tired" imagines taking "a knife / And cut[ting] the world in two," and "Note on Commercial Theatre" complains that white artists have taken Black culture, putting it "in Macbeth and Carmen Jones" and "everything but what's about me." Other clued poems include "Freedom" ("I cannot live on tomorrow's bread"), "One-Way Ticket," "Harlem Night Club," and "April Rain Song."

**Mule Bone (with Zora Neale Hurston)**
A 1930 comic play that Hughes co-wrote with Zora Neale Hurston, based on her folktale "The Bone of Contention." A dispute over its authorship ended their friendship, and the play was not staged until 1991.
